summary.text: The rational root theorem is used to find all the rational roots of a polynomial, if it has any.
It gives a finite number of possible fractions, and each can be checked to see whether it is a root.
When a rational root r is found, the linear factor (x − r) can be divided out by polynomial long division, leaving a polynomial of lower degree.

facts.label: Parent result
facts.value: A special case of Gauss's lemma on factoring polynomials

facts.label: Integral root theorem
facts.value: The special case where the leading coefficient is 1

facts.label: Candidate list
facts.value: A finite number of possible fractions to check

facts.label: After one root
facts.value: Dividing out its linear factor leaves a lower-degree polynomial

facts.label: Cubic bonus
facts.value: A found root leaves a quadratic, avoiding cube roots

items.prompt: There are infinitely many fractions that could be roots of a polynomial. How does the theorem make the hunt manageable?

options.label: It proves every fraction is a root
It narrows the search to a finite list of candidate fractions
It shows that no fraction can ever be a root
It finds the roots without any checking at all

items.explain: The theorem gives a finite number of possible fractions, which can be checked to see whether they are roots.

items.prompt: You find one rational root of a cubic polynomial and divide out its linear factor. What is left to solve?

options.label: Another cubic with one fewer root
A linear polynomial with one root
A quartic that is harder than the original
A quadratic whose two roots are the remaining roots

items.explain: Factoring out the linear factor leaves a quadratic whose two roots, found with the quadratic formula, are the remaining two roots of the cubic.

items.prompt: You test every candidate on a cubic with integer coefficients and none is a root. What is the only way left to express its solutions algebraically?

options.label: Using cube roots
Using only the quadratic formula
Using only whole numbers
They cannot be expressed at all

items.explain: If the test finds no rational solutions, the only way to express the solutions algebraically uses cube roots. A found rational root avoids them.

items.prompt: For a certain polynomial, any rational root must have a numerator that divides 6 and a denominator that divides 1. Which of these cannot be a root?
items.explain: The candidates are limited to ±1, ±2, ±3 and ±6, and 5 does not divide 6.

items.prompt: After finding a rational root, you divide the polynomial by its linear factor using long division. What do you know about the quotient?

options.label: Its degree is higher and it shares no roots with the original
Its degree is the same and it has new roots
Its degree is lower and its roots are also roots of the original
It is always a constant with no roots

items.explain: Dividing out the linear factor gives a polynomial of lower degree whose roots are also roots of the original polynomial.

items.prompt: Every coefficient of a polynomial shares a common whole-number factor. If you divide the whole polynomial by it, does the set of rational roots change?

options.label: Yes, some roots disappear
No, the set of rational roots stays the same
Yes, new roots appear
Yes, all roots become whole numbers

items.explain: Dividing by the greatest common divisor of the coefficients does not alter the set of rational roots.
